The sample `(2 + 3) * 4 / 2` passed syntax validation. This establishes syntax validity only; it does not establish safe evaluation or codebase security. The security tool returned an assessment prompt template, not an audit.

For OWASP-aligned protection:
- Parse expressions with a strict mathematical grammar or an allowlisted AST interpreter. Never pass untrusted expressions to `eval()` or `exec()`.
- Allow only required numeric literals and operators. Reject attributes, imports, comprehensions, arbitrary calls, and unknown names. If functions or variables are needed, explicitly allowlist them and validate their values.
- Enforce input-length, node-count, depth, numeric-magnitude, and exponent limits before expensive operations. Apply execution-time and memory limits in an isolated worker, plus request rate limits.
- Handle division by zero, domain errors, overflow, and non-finite results. Choose numeric precision appropriate to your application.
- Keep variable contexts separate across requests. Return controlled errors, log rejection reasons without sensitive input, and maintain patched dependencies.
- Test valid arithmetic alongside malformed syntax, attribute access, import attempts, huge powers, excessive nesting, and arithmetic errors.

References: [OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [OWASP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

No source code was supplied, so these are implementation recommendations rather than verified findings or a compliance certification.
